raw_case_text:
A 4-year-old male was admitted to the ED of our hospital with generalized urticaria. He had been fishing with his father and, 10 min after lying down on grass, he experienced generalized itchy urticaria and angioedema. Thirty minutes later, on examination in the Emergency Department, urticaria was observed over the entire body and angioedema in his hands.
Benadryl and methylprednisolone were administered. Four hours after treatment, symptoms had stopped, and urticaria and angioedema had disappeared completely.
Two weeks later, he visited a farm. Fifteen minutes after lying down on grass he experienced itching sensations in his hands, arms and trunk, along with generalized erythema. He also complained of congestion/itching in his nose, itchy eyes, and crying. His mother stated that he had slight dyspnea with cough and dizziness. She gave him Benadryl and betamethasone via the oral route based on advice proffered in a previous admission to the ED (which improved the most severe symptoms within 1 h). He was admitted to the ED after 2 h with only erythema, and he received antihistamines for an additional 5 days. The patient had no history of atopy.
By anamnesis, an etiology of insect bites, or intake of food or drugs before these two episodes were excluded. Total Immunoglobulin-E was 123 IU/mL, the blood count and complement (CH50, C3, C4, C1 inhibitor) were normal. Parasitology studies were negative. His mother and maternal grandmother reported a history of allergic rhinitis.
Skin-prick tests (SPTs; Dermaprick ; Alergo Pharma, Buenos Aires, Argentina) were positive to Cynodon dactylis, Phalaris arundinacea and Festuca elatior. Surprisingly these allergens were significantly positive (largest diameter (in mm): 8, 12 and 23, respectively), compared with that of the negative control (1 mm) (Fig. 1). These pollen allergens are used by our research team to ascertain the prevalence of skin sensitivity. 
SPTs were negative for foods (milk, egg, cocoa, citrus fruits, fish, tomatoes, peanuts, wheat, bananas, strawberries) and airborne allergens (Dermatophagoides farinae, D. pteronyssinus, cat dander, dog dander, Alternaria spp., Aspergillus spp., Mucor spp., Cladosporium spp., Penicillium spp., Rhizopus spp., other grasses, weeds, tree pollens).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-year-old boy presented with two acute episodes of generalized pruritic urticaria, hand angioedema, rhinoconjunctivitis, mild dyspnea, cough, and dizziness occurring within 10 to 15 minutes of lying on grass.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: During the first episode, 10 minutes after lying on grass while fishing with his father, the boy developed generalized itchy urticaria and hand angioedema that resolved within 4 hours of emergency department treatment with diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and methylprednisolone. Two weeks later, 15 minutes after lying on grass at a farm, he developed pruritus of the hands, arms, and trunk, generalized erythema, nasal congestion/itching, itchy eyes, crying, mild dyspnea, cough, and dizziness, which partially improved within 1 hour of oral diphenhydramine and betamethasone before ED evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No personal history of atopy, food allergy, drug intake, or insect stings prior to the episodes. Family history positive for allergic rhinitis in his mother and maternal grandmother.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute generalized urticaria, hand angioedema, pruritus, nasal congestion, ocular itching, mild dyspnea, cough, and dizziness upon grass contact.

objective.physical_examination: First ED visit (30 minutes post-exposure): generalized urticaria over the entire body and bilateral hand angioedema. Second ED visit (2 hours post-exposure, after pre-hospital oral antihistamine and corticosteroid): generalized cutaneous erythema.
objective.routine_investigations: Total serum IgE was 123 IU/mL; CBC, complement profile (CH50, C3, C4, C1-esterase inhibitor), and stool parasitology studies were all normal/negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Allergy skin-prick testing (SPT) demonstrated strong positivity to grass pollens—Cynodon dactylon (8 mm wheal), Phalaris arundinacea (12 mm), and Festuca elatior (23 mm) versus 1 mm negative control—and was completely negative for food allergens, dust mites, pet dander, and airborne fungal allergens including Aspergillus spp., Alternaria spp., Mucor spp., Cladosporium spp., Penicillium spp., and Rhizopus spp.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute IgE-mediated contact/environmental grass pollen urticaria, angioedema, and systemic allergic reaction triggered by direct skin contact with grass (Cynodon dactylon, Phalaris arundinacea, and Festuca elatior); fungal sensitization including Aspergillus spp. was excluded by negative skin-prick testing. Managed acutely with oral/parenteral diphenhydramine and corticosteroids (methylprednisolone/betamethasone) followed by a 5-day course of antihistamines and grass avoidance.
